questions.text:
Consider the following statements.

I. Daisy chaining is used to assign priorities in attending interrupts.
II. When a device raises a vectored interrupt, the CPU does polling to identify the source of interrupt.
III. In polling,the CPU periodically checks the status bits to know if any device needs its attention.
IV. During DMA, both the CPU and DMA controller can be bus masters at the same time.

Which of the above statements is/are TRUE?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- I: daisy chaining serially connects devices; the one nearest the CPU gets highest priority [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- II: a vectored interrupt supplies the ISR address itself, so no polling is needed [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- III: that is the definition of polling [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- IV: only one bus master at a time; the CPU gives up the bus during DMA [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.

Answer: I and III only

questions.text: A certain processor deploys a single-level cache. The cache block size is 8 words and the word size is 4 bytes. The memory system uses a 60-MHz clock. To service a cache-miss, the memory controller first takes 1 cycle to accept the starting address of the block, it then takes 3 cycles to fetch all the eight words of the block, and finally transmits the words of the requested block at the rate of 1 word per cycle. The maximum bandwidth for the memory system when the program running on the processor issues a series of read operations is _________[latex]\times 10^6[/latex] bytes/sec.
questions.solution:
One cache miss brings one block of 8 words [latex]\times[/latex] 4 bytes = 32 bytes.
Cycles per block = 1 (address) + 3 (fetch) + 8 (transfer, 1 word per cycle) = 12 cycles.

Time per block = 12 / 60 MHz = 0.2 [latex]\mu[/latex]s.
Bandwidth = 32 bytes / 0.2 [latex]\mu[/latex]s = [latex]160\times10^6[/latex] bytes/s

Answer: 160

questions.text: The chip select logic for a certain DRAM chip in a memory system design is shown below. Assume that the memory system has 16 address lines denoted by [latex]A_{15} \; to \; A_0[/latex]. What is the range of address (in hexadecimal) of the memory system that can get enabled by the chip select (CS) signal?
questions.solution:
CS = 1 only when [latex]A_{15}=1,\ A_{14}=1,\ A_{13}=0,\ A_{12}=0,\ A_{11}=1[/latex] (A13 and A12 enter through inverting bubbles). A10-A0 can be anything.

- Lowest: 1100 1000 0000 0000 = C800
- Highest: 1100 1111 1111 1111 = CFFF

Answer: C800 to CFFF

questions.text: A certain processor uses a fully associative cache of size 16 kB, The cache block size is 16 bytes. Assume that the main memory is byte addressable and uses a 32-bit address. How many bits are required for the Tag and the Index fields respectively in the addresses generated by the processor?
questions.solution:
Fully associative cache has no index field (a block can go in any line).

Block size 16 bytes [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] offset = 4 bits. Tag = 32 [latex]-[/latex] 4 = 28 bits.

Answer: 28 bits and 0 bits

questions.text: For a multi-processor architecture, in which protocol a write transaction is forwarded to only those processors that are known to possess a copy of newly altered cache line?
questions.solution:
A directory-based protocol keeps track of which processors hold each cache line and sends updates/invalidations only to them. Snoopy protocols broadcast to everyone.

Answer: Directory based protocol
